title: Jacob Keyes:
title_short: Jacob Keyes · Somebody Calls, We Come
headline: The tribal chairman who hosted the reception at his own brewery says what safety means where he comes from: somebody calls, we come. Then he says why it is personal.
story: Jacob Keyes is the Chairman of the Iowa Tribe of Oklahoma and the owner of SkyDance Brewing, the Native-owned brewery where the reception was held. He is a guest, not NIWRC staff. He saw violence at home as a child. His answer to “what does safety mean for your community” is one line, and it is the whole video.

Loops: L1 “Who calls, and why does he come?” opens at 0:00 and closes at 0:03 (“My mom dealt with a lot of violence when I was a kid”). L2 “Is anything changing?” opens at 0:00 and closes in the BUTTON (“our youth … that makes me real hopeful”). Stakes: a kid who saw it first hand, communities that still deal with it, and promises the government has not kept.
do: Open on him talking, hook text on frame 1.
Keep his glass out of the crop where you can: push in to chest-up on C1.
Say he is a host and a tribal chairman in the super, nothing more.
Let the mom line sit. Do not cover it with B-roll.
Use only the files named here.
dont: No logo, name or fade at 0:00.
No victim imagery under the mom line. His face, or a plain wide of the patio.
No Tribal affiliation line under his name; his title is his job.
Do not use the “you're going to die” line from his Are You Happy block. That footage belongs to the AYH series.
No somber grade. He is smiling for most of this.

client_note: Why this matters: the client wants real Native people telling the story, with dignity, never as victims. A tribal chairman and business owner saying “we show up” is exactly that.

FILE 26-10-09 C1 Happy - NIWRC Event 11.MP4
[00:01] Interviewee: I'm going to ask you a question and just kind of repeat some of it because they're not going to hear me.
[00:11] Interviewer: First name, last name, title?
[00:13] Interviewee: Jacob Keyes. I'm the chairman of the Iowa Tribe of Oklahoma and the owner and founder of Skydance Peruvian Killers.
[00:22] Interviewer: All right. So what brought you here today, Jacob?
[00:24] Interviewee: Well, these guys wanted to have a great place to have an event,
[00:29] Interviewee: and they obviously wanted to reach out to a Native-owned company,
[00:32] Interviewee: so we were happy to give them some space to have this event.
[00:36] Interviewee: It's really important to us. It's something we try to do as a business here,
[00:40] Interviewee: to reach out into the community and do great things.
[00:42] Interviewee: So here we are. We're looking forward to it.
[00:44] Interviewer: What does safety mean to you?
[00:47] Interviewee: Safety means a lot to me.
[00:49] Interviewer: What these ladies are doing here trying to protect our Native women is important to me.
[00:54] Interviewee: My mom dealt with a lot of violence when I was a kid growing up, so I saw a lot of it firsthand.
[00:60] Interviewee: So it means a lot for us to be able to help bring awareness to that.
[01:05] Interviewee: Our Native communities deal with a lot of that.
[01:07] Interviewer: What does safety mean for your community?
[01:10] Interviewer: Safety for my community?
[01:12] Interviewee: Safety for my community, honestly, it means all of us as a tribe, as a community looking after each other,
[01:18] Interviewee: taking care of each other, being there for each other, always being a quick call away.
[01:22] Interviewee: In the Native community, somebody calls, we come. We show up.
[01:26] Interviewee: So that's kind of really what it means to us.
[01:30] Interviewee: If you could change one thing about Native women and families,
[01:35] Interviewer: if you could change one thing to make Native women and families safer, what would it be?
[01:40] Interviewee: I mean, honestly, I feel like...
[01:42] Interviewee: If I could change one thing to make Native women and families safer.
[01:45] Interviewee: Yeah. I feel like if we could change one thing in our communities for Native women to keep them safe
[01:51] Interviewer: would be if our local governments, our state governments, our federal government
[01:56] Interviewer: could put more resources towards some of our causes like MMIP, things like that
[02:01] Interviewee: that I don't know that people really realize that we deal with those issues as much as we do.
[02:06] Interviewee: So we really need those resources.
[02:08] Interviewee: We need the U.S. government to stick to their promises and their responsibilities
[02:12] Interviewee: to help take care of our communities.
[02:19] Interviewer: What makes you hopeful?
[02:21] Interviewer: Say that again?
[02:22] Interviewer: What makes you hopeful?
[02:23] Interviewee: I mean, what makes me hopeful is seeing all the people that show up to these events
[02:27] Interviewee: and then seeing our youth, our kids.
[02:30] Interviewee: I think now our youth are more involved in these types of causes than they were when I was a kid.
[02:35] Interviewee: There's a lot more awareness. Social media brings a light to a lot of stuff.
[02:38] Interviewee: And so a lot of our youth, I think the future is they're really involved.
[02:42] Interviewee: They really take action and they create these types of organizations.
[02:46] Interviewee: And that makes me real hopeful.
[02:50] Interviewee: So that's it for this section.
[02:52] Interviewee: I'm going to grab a camera.

FILE 26-10-09 C1 Happy - NIWRC Event 12.MP4
[00:00] Interviewee: All right, here we go. So always into here. Here we go. Three, two, go.
[00:07] Interviewee: Say that again.
[00:09] Interviewer: Am I happy?
[00:11] Interviewee: That's the question. I'm always happy. Absolutely.
[00:18] Interviewee: My family is the source of my happiness, my tribe, my community. Those things are the source of my happiness.
[00:26] Interviewee: I mean, I'm just lucky. I have a wife. I've got kids.
[00:29] Interviewee: I've got all of these people that work with me here at the brewery, our tribe at the Iowa tribe.
[00:34] Interviewee: We're all a big huge family and everywhere I go from the time I wake up till I go to bed,
[00:39] Interviewee: I'm surrounded by people that love me. And if you can't be happy with that, then you're just incapable of being happy.
[00:55] Interviewee: Oh my gosh, if I could give one message to the entire world,
[00:58] Interviewee: it would be, this is gonna sound crazy, but it would be that you're going to die.
[01:02] Interviewer: When I say that, what that means is live every day as if this could be the last day of your life.
[01:08] Interviewee: And if you think about it that way, you'll do things, you'll take action.
[01:12] Interviewee: You will do things and make things happen that you never thought of doing before.
[01:17] Interviewee: Good job, man.
